summary: Specifies the Presence Information Data Format, an XML format for presence data used by Common Profile for Presence compliant protocols. It also registers the media type application/pidf+xml for these documents.

plainLanguage.summary: PIDF is a common XML format for sharing presence information, such as whether a contact can receive an instant message. Compatible systems can exchange the document without changing its format.

questions: what does a pidf document look like
subtitle: A common XML document format for presence information shared by compatible protocols.

tldr.problem: Presence systems need a shared way to represent availability and contact information across compatible protocols.
tldr.mechanism: PIDF defines an XML document with a presence root and one or more tuples containing status, optional contact details, notes, timestamps and extensible elements.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines the payload format and registers application/pidf+xml. It leaves transport of the document to each protocol specification.

today: RFC 3863 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the presence data format, not its transport.

sections.title: A Shared Format for Presence
sections.content:
The Common Profile for Presence (CPP) describes operations that help different presence protocols interoperate. RFC 3863 supplies a shared data format, the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF), so presence information can pass between CPP-compliant protocols without modification.

The document defines the data payload and rules for extensions, not how a particular protocol carries it. It defines only a basic status vocabulary and leaves additional status values to separate specifications.
sections.plainLanguage: PIDF gives compatible presence systems a common document to exchange. A separate protocol specification explains how that document travels between systems.

sections.title: The Presence Data Model
sections.content:
Presence information consists of one or more tuples. Each tuple has a status and may include a communication address and other presence data. The document identifies the presentity that published it and permits multiple status values and extensions.

The format also supports a relative priority for contact addresses and a timestamp for when presence data was created. A timestamp can help a receiver recognize older information, even if the message containing it was delayed. XML was selected because the information is hierarchical and must support extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: A PIDF document identifies who published the information and groups details into tuples. A tuple can state availability, provide a contact address and include a creation time.

sections.title: The PIDF XML Structure
sections.content:
The root element is <presence> in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf. It has a required entity attribute containing the presentity's pres URL. The root contains zero or more tuples, then optional notes and extension elements.

Each <tuple> has a unique id for that presentity and a required <status>. It may also contain extensions, a contact, notes and a timestamp. The <basic> status value is either open or closed; for instant messaging these indicate whether the inbox can accept a message.

A contact may have a priority from 0 to 1 inclusive, with at most 3 decimal digits. Higher values mean higher priority. Conforming applications MUST accept UTF-8.
sections.plainLanguage: A PIDF document has a root that names its publisher and contains tuples. Each tuple has a unique ID and status, with optional contact details, notes and a timestamp.

sections.title: Adding Status Information Safely
sections.content:
Applications can add richer presence information using XML namespaces. An extension MUST NOT change the meaning of <basic> or the structure of a PIDF document. A processor MUST ignore elements it does not recognize, including their contents.

An extension can mark a nested element with mustUnderstand when readers need it to interpret a complex extension. Such markers are limited to optional elements inside a status block, so an unknown extension does not prevent a minimal reader from processing basic PIDF information. Standard status extensions in the PIDF status namespace require a Standards Track RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions can add details such as a new status value, but cannot change what open and closed mean. A reader that does not recognize an optional extension skips it and can still process basic status.

sections.title: Privacy, Freshness and Character Encoding
sections.content:
Presence information can be private. A protocol carrying PIDF MUST be able to protect it from eavesdropping, corruption, tampering and replay, including across gateways. The RFC notes that S/MIME can provide protection at the MIME level.

Watchers SHOULD ignore presence information that is older than the latest information they received. Timestamps provide limited replay protection. All conforming processors MUST generate and accept UTF-8; they are strongly discouraged from generating other encodings.
sections.plainLanguage: Presence data may reveal private information, so the protocol carrying it needs end-to-end protection. Timestamps help a reader avoid treating older data as current.

sections.title: Media Type and Namespace Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers the media type application/pidf+xml and two XML namespace URNs: urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf for the base format and urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:pidf:status for standardized status extensions.

The media type can use a charset parameter, and UTF-8 is its default when no parameter is supplied. The registration describes the format as limited use.
sections.plainLanguage: The registrations give the PIDF document and its status extensions stable names. The media type identifies XML content that contains presence information.
